html:
Drag the paddle wheel P0 through the fluid field.

The flow velocity gradients cause the wheel to spin, demonstrating how curl magnitude and direction vary across the field. Near the center, curl is strongest; as you drag outward, notice how it weakens and reverses.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows a physical analogy for the curl of a vector field at a point. At the center is a labeled point P0, around which concentric dashed blue arcs indicate a circular fluid flow pattern. Four paddle-like rectangular surfaces (salmon-colored) radiate outward from P0 like propeller blades. A vertical spindle passes through P0, and the vector Curl F(P0) labels an upward arrow along the spindle, with a curved arrow showing the direction of rotation. The figure provides the physical interpretation that a small paddle wheel immersed in the fluid at P0 rotates most rapidly when its spindle is aligned with curl F(P0), establishing the connection between the curl vector and the direction of maximum circulation density.
authoredInteractions:
- Drag point P₀ to a new location and display the updated Curl F(P₀) vector, showing how curl magnitude and direction vary across the field
- Slider for rotation rate: animate the paddle-wheel spinning and show how the curl vector magnitude corresponds to the angular speed of rotation
- Drag to rotate the 3D viewpoint to see the curl vector axis and paddle blades from any direction
authoredContext: We call curl F(P0) n the circulation density of F at P0 in the direction of n. This quantity has its maximum value when n is in the same direction as curl F(P0); this tells us that at each point in a steady-state fluid flow the maximum circulation density occurs in the direction of the curl. Physically, this means that if a small paddle wheel is immersed in the fluid so that the pivot point is at P0, then the paddles will turn most rapidly when the spindle is aligned with curl F(P0) (Figure 15.8.6). If curl F = 0 at each point of a region, then F is said to be irrotational in that region, since no circulation occurs about any point of the region
sourceQmd: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 15.8.6

discrepancies: The flow lines are dashed concentric circles in the generated figure, whereas they are solid continuous arcs in the source figure.
The generated figure includes a fixed-length vertical spindle that overlaps and visually interferes with the dynamically scaling curl vector arrow, whereas the source integrates them.
The circular rotation arrow is rendered as a thicker 3D tube in the generated figure instead of a thin line as seen in the source.
The generated figure lacks the small arrows on the flow lines that indicate the direction of the fluid flow.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure accurately captures the paddle wheel analogy for curl and adds an excellent interactive element to explore a vector field, though some minor aesthetic details differ from the source.
action_items: Change the concentric flow lines from LineDashedMaterial to a solid LineBasicMaterial to match the source figure.
Remove or dynamically scale the fixed vertical spindle so it does not awkwardly overlap or extend beyond the curl vector arrow when the curl magnitude changes.
Reduce the thickness of the circular rotation arrow's tube geometry so it closer resembles a thin curved line.
